questions.prompt: Find the shortest distance between the parallel lines A and B in the figure. A passes through (0,0) with slope 1; B passes through (0,-2) and (2,0).

questions.theory: The shortest segment joining two parallel lines is perpendicular to both. If their equations share coefficients a and b, their distance is |c1-c2|/sqrt(a²+b²). The denominator normalizes the normal vector (a,b); simply subtracting intercepts usually measures a vertical or horizontal segment instead. Equations must be scaled consistently before applying the formula. The graphical points determine slope and intercept, and the calculation then avoids errors from drawing scale. Rotating or translating the coordinate system cannot change the perpendicular separation. For lines of slope 1, vertical separation is sqrt(2) times the true distance.

questions.prompt: Exactly one of A,B,C,D committed a crime. A and D always tell the truth; B and C always lie. C and D are indistinguishable twins. A says “D is innocent”; B says “A is guilty”; one twin says “A is innocent” and the other “B is guilty”. Which statement is FALSE?
hints: Use the statements of the two identified speakers first.
A is innocent, so which twin could truthfully say otherwise?
questions.solution: A is truthful, so D is innocent. B lies, so A is innocent. Therefore the twin saying “A is innocent” must be D, and the twin saying “B is guilty” must be C. The latter statement is false, so B is innocent. Since exactly one suspect is guilty, C is guilty. A, B and C are true statements; D is the false statement.
questions.theory: Truth-teller problems translate each utterance into a proposition and a truth value fixed by its speaker. A liar’s statement is false; that does not mean every word in it changes independently. Start with speakers whose identities are known, then use resulting facts to identify anonymous speakers. The condition that exactly one person committed the crime is a separate logical constraint, used after innocence has been established. Here the truth value of “A is innocent” distinguishes the identical twins even though their appearance does not. Avoid assuming that a guilty person lies or an innocent person tells the truth: guilt and truthfulness are independent properties in the premises.

similar_questions.solution: P is innocent by truthfulness, so Q is guilty by exclusivity.

Quadrupeds include reptiles as well as mammals, while mammals include whales and humans that are not quadrupeds in the ordinary sense. These examples establish proper overlap. The two smaller named categories are disjoint and each belongs to exactly one of the larger categories. questions.prompt: Water is filled into a cone from the top at a constant volumetric rate. The rate of increase of the height of the water column:

options.B: Depends on the apex angle of the cone.
options.C: Increases as the cube root of the volumetric rate.
options.D: Increases as the square root of the volumetric rate.

hints: Express water volume using height and the cone half-angle.
Compare rates at fixed height and at fixed elapsed time: these are different comparisons.
questions.solution: This single-answer question lacks a specified comparison. For an initially empty cone with downward vertex and half-angle $\theta$, $Qt=(\pi\tan^2\theta/3)h^3$. Therefore $\dot h=(1/3)[3Q/(\pi\tan^2\theta)]^{1/3}t^{-2/3}$. Both B and C are true at fixed elapsed time. At fixed height, $\dot h=Q/(\pi h^2\tan^2\theta)$, so B is true but C is not. A and D do not match either formula. A unique graded answer requires specifying what is held fixed and the cone orientation/initial condition.
questions.theory: Related-rate problems must distinguish a rate as a function of position from the same rate as a function of time. For a cone with water starting at its vertex, similarity gives radius r=h tan(theta), and volume is pi h³ tan²(theta)/3. Differentiating volume with respect to time yields Q=A(h)h-dot, where A is the cross-sectional area. Integrating the constant inflow gives a second formula involving elapsed time and the initial water volume. Scaling Q at fixed h is linear, whereas scaling it at fixed elapsed time from empty is a cube-root law. An unstated comparison can therefore make apparently competing options simultaneously true.

similar_questions.prompt: In a cone with tan(theta)=1 and Q=pi, find h(t) from empty.
similar_questions.solution: h³=3t, hence h=(3t)^(1/3) and h-dot=(3t)^(-2/3).

similar_questions.prompt: At h=2 in the same cone, compare Q=pi and Q=8pi.
similar_questions.solution: h-dot=Q/(pi h²): rates are 1/4 and 2, a factor of 8.

questions.prompt: The source graph gives the wavelength-dependent absorbance of compounds A and B. Mixture absorbance is linear in their concentrations. R is absorbance at 650 nm divided by absorbance at 950 nm. If the mixture contains 95% A, what is R?
hints: Use a concentration-weighted sum at each wavelength.
The graph shows A much lower at 650 than 950; only 5% of the strongly absorbing B is present.
questions.solution: Write $R=[0.95a_{650}+0.05b_{650}]/[0.95a_{950}+0.05b_{950}]$. The plotted heights give a smaller numerator than denominator: A rises substantially between the two wavelengths, while the small 5% contribution from B does not offset that rise. Thus R<1, D. The composition percentages themselves are not absorbance ratios, rejecting A and B; equality in C is also inconsistent with the plotted weighted heights.
questions.theory: Absorbance additivity means that each compound’s pure-spectrum height is multiplied by its concentration fraction before the contributions are summed. The ratio of sums is not a sum of ratios, nor does a 95% concentration imply a ratio of 95. A spectrum can be used qualitatively when its relative heights clearly establish an inequality. If numerical absorbances are absent, the graph cannot specify the precise ratio, but can still distinguish whether it lies below or above one. The condition for R<1 is 0.95(a950-a650)>0.05(b650-b950). This explicitly identifies the two competing spectral changes and explains why concentration weighting is essential.

questions.prompt: In a population P, disease spread rate R is proportional to both affected population N and unaffected population P-N. Which source graph is correct?

In a closed epidemic model the number of unaffected people is P-N, not a separate constant. The product N(P-N) captures both scarcity of infectious people at the beginning and scarcity of susceptible people at the end. Its second derivative is negative and its first derivative vanishes at N=P/2. This determines the graph without solving for N as a function of time. A logistic population curve plots N against time, while this question plots its rate against N; confusing those axes is a common mistake.

questions.prompt: A and B finish a job in 30 days; B and C in 24 days; C and A in 28 days. Which conclusion is correct?

options.A: C is most efficient and B least.
options.B: B is most efficient; the least cannot be determined.
options.C: C is most efficient; the least cannot be determined.
options.D: C is most efficient and A least.

hints: Let individual daily work rates be a,b,c.
Subtract pairwise-rate equations instead of comparing days directly.
questions.solution: The rates satisfy a+b=1/30, b+c=1/24, c+a=1/28. Subtracting gives c-a=1/120>0 and c-b=1/420>0; also b-a=1/168>0. Hence c>b>a. D is correct. A misidentifies the least efficient, B the most efficient, and C incorrectly says the least is undetermined.
questions.theory: For independent workers on the same job, daily completion fractions add. A completion time t corresponds to rate 1/t, so fewer days means larger rate. Three pairwise totals determine three individual rates uniquely by linear equations. Even when only ordering is needed, subtracting two equations isolates a difference of individual rates and avoids unnecessary arithmetic. This assumes the workers’ efficiencies remain constant and their combined work is additive. Comparing pair completion times directly with individual worker names is unreliable because each pair shares a different colleague. Positivity of derived rates is a useful consistency check for any numerical work-rate problem.

questions.theory: Water density depends on temperature and dissolved salt concentration. Over the temperatures shown, thermal expansion makes warmer water less dense. Adding salt increases mass per volume and raises density. When one sample dominates another in both favorable directions, its ordering does not require a quantitative density formula. If temperature and salinity changes compete, however, a formula or additional information is needed to decide the result. The low-temperature density anomaly of pure water near 4°C does not apply to the 12–16°C comparison here. questions.prompt: A boat weighs 60 kg. Oarsmen A and B weigh 80 and 90 kg. At constant power, course time is proportional to total weight. Alone they finish in 1 hour and 1½ hours, respectively. Their powers add. Find their joint time.
hints: Use t=K W/P for the fixed course.
Infer each power from its solo total weight, including the boat.
questions.solution: Write t=K W/P. Thus P_A/K=140/1=140 and P_B/K=150/1.5=100. Together W=230 and (P_A+P_B)/K=240, giving t=230/240 hours=57.5 minutes. B is correct; A,C,D do not follow the additive-power calculation.
questions.theory: The stated model separates total carried weight and applied power for a fixed course: time is proportional to weight and inversely proportional to power. Solo completion times must include the boat’s mass as well as the rower’s. When rowers combine, powers add while the boat is counted only once. Ordinary work-rate addition is not directly applicable because the carried weight changes between solo and joint trials. Introducing a shared constant K lets it cancel after the powers have been inferred in common units. Checking units helps: weight divided by power has time units up to the same course constant, and final hours must be converted to minutes.

similar_questions.prompt: If a 100 kg total load takes 2 h, how long for 150 kg at twice the power?

questions.prompt: A parallelogram ABCD has base length a, height h, centre O, and E the midpoint of CD. Find area of triangle OAE.
hints: Use an affine coordinate system for the parallelogram.
The determinant of the two triangle edge vectors gives the area fraction.
questions.solution: Set C=0, D=u, B=v, A=u+v, where |det(u,v)|=ah. Then E=u/2 and O=(u+v)/2. The edge vectors A-E=u/2+v and O-E=v/2 have determinant det(u,v)/4. Triangle area is half its magnitude, ah/8. C is correct; the other fractions are different.
questions.theory: Area ratios in a parallelogram are preserved by affine transformations, so a skew drawing need not be treated with trigonometry. Choose its two side vectors as a coordinate basis. Midpoints and the centre then have simple vector expressions, and the determinant of two edge vectors gives the oriented parallelogram area. A triangle has half that area. The physical side length b is irrelevant because the total area is already given by base times perpendicular height. A common mistake is to apply a triangle’s half-area factor twice without identifying its actual base and altitude, or to use the slanted side as the height.

similar_questions.solution: The affine-invariant fraction is 1/8, so area=10.

similar_questions.prompt: Triangle ACD in a parallelogram has what area?
similar_questions.solution: Its base CD is a and altitude h, so area=ah/2.

questions.prompt: The sum of the first n positive even integers is:

options.A: Divisible by n but not n+1.
options.B: Divisible by n+1 but not n.
options.C: Divisible by both n and n+1.
options.D: Divisible by neither n nor n+1.

hints: Factor 2 out of the sum.
Use the formula for 1+2+⋯+n.
questions.solution: The sum is 2(1+2+⋯+n)=2n(n+1)/2=n(n+1). For every positive integer n, both n and n+1 divide this product. C is correct; A,B,D deny one or both explicit factors.
questions.theory: A sum of consecutive terms in an arithmetic progression equals the number of terms times the average of its first and last terms. The first n positive even integers are 2,4,…,2n, so their average is n+1 and their sum is n(n+1). Divisibility is easiest to establish by factoring rather than examining selected small values. Showing an integer m divides a quantity means expressing it as m times an integer. Both factors are positive integers here. The question concerns universal statements for all positive n; a single numerical example cannot prove them, though it can expose an incorrect claim.

questions.prompt: On a 200 m straight road, the maximum number of poles are placed at 20 m intervals. How many must be removed to retain the maximum number at 40 m intervals?

questions.theory: For a closed line segment, equally spaced points include both endpoints when length is an integer multiple of spacing. Therefore m intervals require m+1 points. Counting objects and gaps interchangeably causes the usual off-by-one error. Doubling the spacing retains every other original pole. Starting at an endpoint achieves the maximum count here; starting at 20 m retains only five poles because neither endpoint is included. Both counts must use the same endpoint convention before subtraction. This differs from points around a closed circular track, where the number of equal gaps equals the number of points rather than one less.

questions.prompt: For subsets $E_n\subset\mathbb R$, define $\limsup E_n=\bigcap_{k=1}^\infty\bigcup_{n=k}^\infty E_n$ and $\liminf E_n=\bigcup_{k=1}^\infty\bigcap_{n=k}^\infty E_n$. Which statement is true?

options.C: $\liminf E_n=\{x:x\in E_n\text{ for all finitely many }n\}$.

hints: Translate the intersections and unions into quantifiers.
The correct liminf description is “for all but finitely many n”; compare the exact printed wording.
questions.solution: The formulas give $x\in\limsup E_n$ iff every tail contains an index with x in E_n, equivalently infinitely many memberships. They give $x\in\liminf E_n$ iff x belongs to every E_n after some index. A fails for alternating empty/{0} sets; B fails for E_1={0} and E_n=∅ thereafter; D describes limsup. C prints “for all finitely many n”, which is not “for all BUT finitely many n” and has no standard quantified meaning. If “but” were supplied C would be correct, but the printed question has no unambiguous answer.
questions.theory: Set limits are membership-based operations, not topological limits of points. Limsup contains points appearing infinitely often; liminf contains points appearing eventually always. The inclusion liminf⊆limsup holds without any regularity assumption. Equality occurs when each point’s membership eventually stabilizes, as with increasing or decreasing sets. A union over all indices requires only one membership, whereas an intersection of tail unions requires memberships arbitrarily far out. An existential tail followed by universal membership is different again. Exact quantifiers matter: “finitely many” and “all but finitely many” express almost opposite behavior. This is why a missing word cannot safely be repaired when assigning a graded answer.

questions.prompt: Let $p\ge1$ be an integer and $r(t)=e^{it}$, $0\le t\le2\pi$. Let f be holomorphic on $|z|<R$, R>1, with its only zero at $z_0$, $0<|z_0|<R$, of multiplicity q. Evaluate $(2\pi i)^{-1}\int_r [f\prime(z)/f(z)]z^p\,dz$.
hints: Locate the zero relative to the unit circle, not merely the radius R.
The logarithmic derivative has residue q at a zero of multiplicity q.
questions.solution: Locally $f(z)=(z-z_0)^qh(z)$ with h nonzero, so $f\prime/f=q/(z-z_0)+h\prime/h$. If |z_0|<1 the residue theorem gives qz_0^p, option A. If 1<|z_0|<R, the integrand is holomorphic inside the contour and the integral is 0, absent from all options. If |z_0|=1, it is singular on the contour and the ordinary integral is undefined. The hypothesis permits all three cases, so A cannot be asserted universally; B–D are not the residue formula either.
questions.theory: The logarithmic derivative f-prime/f has a simple pole at each zero, with residue equal to its multiplicity. Multiplying by a holomorphic weight g changes that residue to multiplicity times g at the zero. The residue theorem sums only singularities enclosed by the actual integration contour, and requires no singularity on that contour. A disk of holomorphy larger than the unit disk does not imply that its zeros lie inside the unit circle. Holomorphy of f itself on the contour also does not make f-prime/f regular there when f vanishes. These localization conditions are indispensable in weighted versions of the argument principle.

questions.prompt: For positive integer k, consider $y\prime=y^{5k/(5k+2)}$ for t>0, y(0)=0. Which assertion about C¹ solutions on (0,∞) is true?
hints: The exponent α=5k/(5k+2) is between 0 and 1.
Construct solutions that remain zero until an arbitrary waiting time.
questions.solution: Let α=5k/(5k+2). For every T≥0, define y_T(t)=0 for t≤T and $[(1-\alpha)(t-T)]^{1/(1-\alpha)}$ for t>T. Since 1/(1-α)=(5k+2)/2>1, both y and its derivative join continuously at T. Direct differentiation verifies the ODE on both sides. Different T give infinitely many solutions, including the zero solution. C is true; A,B,D are contradicted.
questions.theory: Continuity of the right-hand side ensures existence locally, but uniqueness generally requires local Lipschitz regularity in the dependent variable. A power y^α with 0<α<1 is not locally Lipschitz at zero, since its derivative grows without bound there. Separation is valid on a positive branch and gives y=[(1-α)(t-T)]^(1/(1-α)). The branch can be joined to the zero solution at any waiting time because its first derivative vanishes at the join. Dividing by y^α before considering y=0 would discard these solutions. The construction uses only nonnegative y and therefore avoids issues about defining fractional powers for negative arguments.

similar_questions.prompt: Solve y-prime=sqrt(y), y(0)=0 with waiting time T.
similar_questions.solution: y=0 until T and y=(t-T)²/4 afterward; every T≥0 gives a C¹ solution.

similar_questions.prompt: Does y-prime=y, y(0)=0 admit such waiting solutions?
similar_questions.solution: No. The right side is Lipschitz, and the unique solution is identically zero.

questions.theory: For autonomous power equations with positive initial values, separation of variables produces explicit maximal solutions. The sign of the vector field determines whether the solution increases or decreases, while the exponent α>1 makes growth fast enough to blow up in finite time. Eliminating the family parameter is legitimate on regular regions where the required division is defined, and scaling a vector field by a nonzero factor preserves its integral curves. Every smooth function of its invariants is constant along those curves. Degenerate points require local care, but do not change the listed general family on regular regions.

Absolute values lose sign information globally, but on a fixed quadrant they differ from x/y by a constant sign and describe the same arbitrary-function family. questions.prompt: Let f be infinitely differentiable on a bounded interval I. Fix n>1 distinct nodes x0,…,x(n-1), and add nodes x(n+j)=xj+ε, all 2n nodes distinct. Let p(2n-1) be their Lagrange polynomial and q(2n-1) the Hermite polynomial matching f and f′ at the original n nodes. As ε→0, what happens to sup over I of |p-q|?
hints: Replace each pair of interpolation conditions by a value and a divided difference.
The divided difference tends to f′ at its fixed node.
questions.solution: The conditions p(xj)=f(xj) and [p(xj+ε)-p(xj)]/ε=[f(xj+ε)-f(xj)]/ε tend to p(xj)=f(xj), p′(xj)=f′(xj). The limiting Hermite system is nonsingular for distinct original nodes. Therefore the 2n polynomial coefficients converge to those of q. Because I is bounded and the degree is fixed, coefficient convergence gives uniform convergence on I. The supremum tends to zero: C; A,B,D are false.
questions.theory: Hermite interpolation is the confluent limit of ordinary interpolation when distinct nodes merge in pairs. Replacing nearly repeated value equations with divided-difference equations reveals a stable limiting linear system. Its uniqueness follows because a polynomial of degree at most 2n-1 vanishing with its derivative at n distinct nodes would be divisible by a degree-2n product of squared factors, so must be zero. Continuity of the resulting finite matrix inverse gives coefficient convergence as nodes coalesce. Fixed polynomial degree and bounded evaluation interval turn coefficient convergence into uniform convergence. No claim about increasingly high interpolation degree is made; that separate limit can behave very differently.

This necessary condition assumes the needed derivatives exist. Here the derivative-square term makes the equation linear and its two integration constants are determined by two boundary conditions. A stationary curve is not automatically a minimum; the positive second variation or strict convexity supplies that conclusion in this case. Factors in the derivative of 2(y-prime)² are easy to miss: F_y-prime is 4y-prime, not 2y-prime. Substituting candidate second derivatives quickly rejects distractors.

questions.prompt: A constant-density solid is the unit upper hemisphere $S=\{(x,y,z):x^2+y^2+z^2\le1,z\ge0\}$. Which statement is true?

options.C: The inertia tensor is not diagonal.
options.D: The z-axis is a principal axis.

hints: Use reflections x↦-x and y↦-y to examine products of inertia.
Both coordinate axes named in the options are eigenvector directions of a diagonal tensor.
questions.solution: The centre of mass is (0,0,3/8), so A is false. By x and y reflection symmetry, ∫xy,∫xz,∫yz all vanish, so the inertia tensor about the origin is diagonal. Indeed each diagonal entry is 4πρ/15. Thus both B and D are true and C false. About the centre of mass, the shifted tensor remains diagonal, with x and z still principal directions. Part B requires one answer but the source supplies two true assertions, so this is ungraded.
questions.theory: The inertia tensor has diagonal entries given by integrals of sums of two squared coordinates and off-diagonal entries equal to minus products of inertia. A principal direction is an eigenvector of this symmetric tensor. Reflection symmetries force products of inertia involving an odd reflected coordinate to vanish. Translating the reference point along a symmetry axis changes diagonal moments through the parallel-axis theorem but preserves the coordinate principal directions. For a hemisphere, the centre of mass is displaced from the sphere centre; this does not prevent the tensor from being diagonal. Rotational symmetry determines equivalent horizontal directions, and the vertical symmetry axis is also principal.

questions.prompt: A student solves 50% of questions, getting these correct with probability 0.90, and guesses the rest, getting guesses correct with probability 0.30. Given a correct answer, find the probability it was guessed.
hints: Distinguish P(correct|guess) from P(guess|correct).
Use Bayes with the two equal prior branches.
questions.solution: P(correct)=0.5·0.3+0.5·0.9=0.6. P(guess and correct)=0.15, so P(guess|correct)=0.15/0.6=0.25. A is correct. B is the prior guessing probability, C is success when solving, and D reverses the conditioning.
questions.theory: Bayes’ theorem reverses conditional probabilities by multiplying the likelihood by the prior and dividing by total evidence probability. The categories guessed and solved partition the attempts, so the law of total probability adds their two contributions to correctness. Correct answers disproportionately come from the more successful solved category even though half the attempts are guesses. Conditioning must be read in order: the probability of correctness given guessing is not the probability of guessing given correctness. A probability tree or a hypothetical count of 100 attempts makes the denominator clear: 15 correct guesses and 45 correct solved answers produce 60 total correct answers.

questions.solution: The central limit theorem gives $(\sum X_i-5n)/\sqrt n\Rightarrow N(0,10)$. For nonzero a the limit is N(0,10a²), standard normal when a=±1/√10, so C is true. For a=0 the random variable is identically zero for every n, giving a degenerate limit, so D is also true. questions.theory: A chi-square variable with ν degrees of freedom has mean ν and variance 2ν. Independent identically distributed variables with finite positive variance satisfy the classical central limit theorem after centering and scaling by sqrt(n). Multiplication by a fixed constant scales the limiting variance by its square, including a negative constant because a centred normal law is symmetric. Zero scaling is exceptional: it destroys all randomness and yields a point mass, which is a degenerate distribution. The phrase “for an appropriate a” is existential, so both a nonzero standardizing constant and zero must be considered if the domain includes all real constants.

questions.prompt: In a Markov chain, i and j communicate. Which assertion is NOT correct?

options.B: i is recurrent iff j is recurrent.
options.C: lim P(Xn=i|X0=k)=lim P(Xn=j|X0=k) for every k.

hints: Period and recurrence are communication-class properties.
Check whether the displayed ordinary limits exist without aperiodicity.
questions.solution: A and B are valid class properties. C fails even for an aperiodic irreducible two-state chain with identical rows (1/3,2/3): the two limits are 1/3 and 2/3. D is valid when the relevant limits exist in the usual aperiodic setting, but no existence assumption is stated. For the alternating chain P=[[0,1],[1,0]], i and j communicate while both sequences in D oscillate and lack limits. Therefore C is an intended counterexample, but D is not a universally meaningful true assertion under the printed assumptions. The literal single-choice question is ungraded.
questions.theory: Communication means each state can reach the other in finitely many transitions with positive probability. Period, recurrence and positive recurrence are properties shared across a communicating class. Transition probabilities to different destination states need not have the same limiting value; in an irreducible positive recurrent aperiodic chain they approach the corresponding stationary probabilities. Transition probabilities from different starting states to one fixed destination do converge to the same value under those conditions. Periodicity can destroy ordinary limits entirely, although Cesàro averages may still converge. Consequently a theorem stated with plain limits must establish their existence or add aperiodicity rather than silently treating oscillating sequences as convergent.

questions.solution: Let r_i be the mean in row i, c_j the mean in column j, and g the grand mean. The constraints give E(r_i-g)=β_i and E(c_j-g)=γ_j. Therefore A is estimated by r1-g, B by c1-g, C by r1-r2, and D by r1+c2-2g. All four are estimable. The source is Part B and permits one answer only, so it cannot be graded as printed. Omitting the constraints would change the identification problem, but they are explicitly present.
questions.theory: Estimability asks whether a parameter function has a linear unbiased estimator under the stated model. Unconstrained additive ANOVA has redundant parameterizations, so individual effects are not identifiable without normalization. Zero-sum constraints resolve that redundancy by defining the grand mean and deviations uniquely. In a complete two-way table, row and column averages isolate those deviations after subtracting the grand average. Every linear combination of identifiable effects is then estimable. The covariance assumptions determine estimator variances and optimality but are not needed to verify these expectation identities. Always check whether constraints are part of the model before applying general statements about nonestimable individual ANOVA effects.

questions.prompt: A simple random sample without replacement of n=10 is taken from N=100. The printed sample variance is $s^2=(1/10)\sum_{i=1}^{10}(y_i-\bar y)^2$. An unbiased estimate of the printed population quantity $\sigma^2=(1/10)\sum_{i=1}^{100}(Y_i-\bar Y)^2$ is:

The usual sample variance with divisor n-1 is unbiased for the population divisor N-1.
questions.solution: Write T=∑(Y_i-Ȳ)². Under SRSWOR, E[s²]=(n-1)T/[n(N-1)]=9T/(10·99)=T/110. The printed target is T/10, so the unbiased estimator is 11s². None of A–D equals 11s². Even replacing the target divisor 10 by the conventional 100 would require (11/10)s², also absent. The source therefore has a substantive normalization/option error and is ungraded.
questions.theory: Finite-population variance has two common conventions: T/N and T/(N-1), where T is the sum of squared deviations about the population mean. Under sampling without replacement, the sample variance with divisor n-1 estimates T/(N-1) without bias. Using divisor n instead multiplies its expectation by (n-1)/n. To estimate any stated target, first express both its expectation and the target in terms of the same T, then take their ratio. The finite population correction belongs to the variance of a sample mean, not this bias adjustment. Literal denominators are essential; replacing an unusual definition with a familiar convention changes the mathematical question.

questions.prompt: Let f(x,y)=2xy/(x²+y²) off (0,0), and f(0,0)=0. Define $g(x,y)=\sum_{n=1}^\infty 2^{-n}f(x-n,y-n)$. Which statements are true?

hints: Use |2xy|≤x²+y² to bound every summand.
A translated summand is discontinuous only at its own diagonal lattice point, while its vertical sections are continuous.
questions.solution: Since |f|≤1, the series converges uniformly by comparison with ∑2^-n. Every vertical section of f is continuous, including the section x=0, which is identically zero. Thus A holds by uniform convergence. Each summand is continuous off its translated origin, giving D. At (k,k), the kth summand has value 0 but tends to 2^-k along the diagonal; the uniformly convergent remaining sum is continuous there. Hence g is discontinuous at every such point, rejecting B, and uniform absolute convergence rejects C.
questions.theory: Uniform convergence follows from a summable majorant independent of the input, known as the Weierstrass M-test. Uniform limits preserve continuity when the component functions are continuous on the domain under consideration. They do not repair a discontinuity of one summand when the remaining sum is continuous there. Separate continuity means continuity in one variable while the other is held fixed; it is weaker than joint continuity in several variables. The base function here is a standard bounded separately continuous function that lacks a joint limit at the origin. Translating and summing it creates countably many isolated discontinuities without destroying its continuous one-dimensional sections.

questions.solution: A=1 on [0,1) and A(1)=0, so its continuous partial sums cannot converge uniformly to this discontinuous limit. B=(1-x)/(1+x) throughout [0,1], including its zero endpoint. Its remainder has magnitude (1-x)x^(N+1)/(1+x)≤(1-x)x^(N+1), whose maximum is (N+1)^(N+1)/(N+2)^(N+2)→0. Thus both converge pointwise and only B uniformly: A,D true; B,C false.
questions.theory: Uniform convergence controls the largest error over the whole domain, rather than errors at each fixed point separately. A sequence of continuous functions with a discontinuous pointwise limit cannot converge uniformly. A continuous limit alone does not prove uniform convergence, so the alternating series needs an explicit remainder bound. Geometric sums make that bound available even near the endpoint where x is close to one. The factor 1-x forces the alternating remainder to shrink uniformly, whereas the nonalternating series accumulates an endpoint jump. At x=1 every summand is exactly zero; applying the formula for x<1 without checking that endpoint gives a wrong limit.

questions.prompt: Real-valued functions fn on ℝ converge to a continuous f uniformly on every closed bounded subset. Which conclusions follow?

options.C: All sufficiently large fn are bounded.
options.D: All sufficiently large fn are continuous.

hints: Put a particular x in a compact interval.
Uniform local convergence need not transfer regularity backward to approximants.
questions.solution: For each x, uniform convergence on [x-1,x+1] implies fn(x)→f(x), proving B. A fails for fn(x)=x/n→0 locally uniformly, whose global errors are unbounded. The same example disproves C. D fails for fn=(1/n)1_ℚ: these are discontinuous everywhere but converge uniformly to the continuous zero function. Thus only B follows.
questions.theory: Locally uniform convergence means uniform convergence on every compact subset, with the required index allowed to depend on that subset. It always implies pointwise convergence. The continuity theorem for uniform limits has a one-way hypothesis: continuous approximants imply a continuous limit. A continuous limit does not force its approximants to be continuous.
